records.title: Feature is proactive, not triggered by a specific incident
records.summary: The rewards platform team is proactively building a feature to handle reward points seamlessly across credit card upgrades; no specific customer complaint or incident was cited as the trigger.

records.title: Competitive research on reward-point continuity is explicitly desired
records.summary: The team explicitly wants to see how other platforms handle reward points during a credit card upgrade, to inform this feature.

records.title: Current reward-point handling during a card upgrade is assumed not seamless
records.summary: The team's stated goal ("handled seamlessly") implies today's handling of reward points during a credit card upgrade is not seamless. Now validated: the transfer is a manual operations process, not an automated one.

data.statement: Today, when a customer upgrades their credit card, their accrued reward points are not handled seamlessly — some unspecified friction, loss, delay, or manual process currently occurs.
data.impact_if_wrong: If current handling is already adequate, effort could be misdirected toward a problem that doesn't concretely exist, or aimed at the wrong part of the experience.

records.title: Reward points are currently transferred manually by operations
records.summary: When a customer upgrades their credit card today, an operations team manually transfers their accrued reward points — there is no automated handling in place.

records.title: Manual ops transfer is a scaling and error-risk bottleneck
records.summary: Because reward-point transfers during a card upgrade are handled manually by operations today, the process is bottlenecked on that team's capacity and exposed to human error/delay, with no stated safeguard as upgrade volume grows.

records.title: Chase: Ultimate Rewards balance carries over automatically on product change
records.summary: Chase carries a cardmember's Ultimate Rewards points balance over automatically when they product-change to another Ultimate Rewards-earning card, with no manual transfer step.

data.claim: When a Chase cardmember does a product change (upgrade or downgrade) to another Ultimate Rewards-earning card, their existing Ultimate Rewards points balance carries over automatically, with no manual transfer step and no loss of the underlying point balance.

records.details: Chase can likely guarantee automatic, no-manual-step continuity here because Ultimate Rewards points are a single shared currency/ledger across all Ultimate-Rewards-earning Chase cards rather than a per-product balance — a product change re-labels which card is attached to the account without touching the underlying points ledger, so there is nothing for an ops team to reconcile.

sources.label: Chase - Credit Card Product Changes: A Quick Guide
CreditCards.com - How to upgrade a Chase credit card

records.title: Chase: redemption value is gated by current card tier, not the point balance itself
records.summary: After downgrading off a premium Chase card, the point balance is preserved but access to transfer partners and boosted portal redemption rates is lost.

data.claim: After a Chase product change/downgrade off a premium card (e.g., Sapphire Preferred) onto a card marketed as cash back (e.g., Freedom), the cardmember keeps their Ultimate Rewards point balance but loses access to transfer partners and the boosted travel-portal redemption rate that the premium card provided.

records.details: Chase funds transfer-partner relationships and the elevated portal redemption rate through the annual fee on its premium cards, so it gates those specific redemption options to whichever card a customer currently holds rather than to the points themselves — this protects the fee-supported revenue model while still letting the point balance itself move freely, since the balance and its redemption value are tracked separately.

sources.label: CreditCards.com - How to upgrade a Chase credit card
FinanceBuzz - Chase Sapphire Cards downgrade guide

records.title: Amex: upgrades restricted to staying within the same reward-currency family
records.summary: American Express does not allow a card upgrade/downgrade to cross between cash back and Membership Rewards currencies.

data.claim: American Express only permits card upgrades/downgrades within the same card 'family' — a cardmember holding a cash back-earning card (e.g., Blue Cash Everyday) cannot product-change into a Membership Rewards-earning card (e.g., Amex Gold), or vice versa.

records.details: Cash back on Amex cards is a direct monetary rebate/statement-credit liability tracked in dollars, while Membership Rewards points are a separate proprietary loyalty currency with its own transfer-partner and breakage economics. Allowing a customer to cross from one to the other would force Amex to define and defend a conversion rate between two differently-modeled liabilities, so Amex avoids that accounting and financial-exposure complexity by hard-walling upgrades to stay within one reward-currency family.

sources.label: CreditCards.com - How to upgrade an American Express card

records.title: Citi: product changes reportedly blocked between AAdvantage and ThankYou card families
records.summary: Citi has, per multiple third-party reports, restricted product changes between its AAdvantage-branded (airline miles) cards and its ThankYou Points-branded cards.

data.claim: Citi has restricted product changes so that a cardmember cannot move directly between an AAdvantage-branded (airline miles) card and a ThankYou Points-branded card in either direction — the two reward currencies are treated as separate product families for product-change purposes.

records.details: AAdvantage miles earned on Citi's co-branded cards are issued under a partnership agreement with American Airlines rather than being Citi's own currency, while ThankYou Points are Citi's proprietary currency. Letting a customer product-change across that boundary would require Citi to either buy back miles already committed to the airline partnership or invent a conversion rate between two currencies with very different unit costs, so Citi keeps the two families walled off from each other. Confidence is medium rather than high because third-party reporting on this rule has been inconsistent over time, with some reports describing Citi loosening the restriction again after tightening it.

sources.label: Doctor Of Credit - Citi no longer allowing product changes between AAdvantage & ThankYou

records.title: Capital One: self-service, one-directional cash-back-to-miles conversion
records.summary: Capital One lets cardmembers self-convert cash back into miles at a fixed rate, one direction only, rather than automatically as part of a product change.

data.claim: Capital One lets a cardmember move earned cash back into Capital One miles via a self-service 'Combine Rewards' action at a fixed rate of 1 cent of cash back per mile, but the conversion only runs in that one direction — miles cannot be converted back into cash back at that same rate — and it requires the cardmember to hold both a cash back card and a miles-eligible card (e.g., Venture or Venture X) rather than happening as an automatic side-effect of a product change.

records.details: Making the cross-currency conversion self-service, one-directional, and fixed-rate lets Capital One offer more cross-currency flexibility than Amex or Citi allow, without opening a two-way arbitrage loophole or requiring an ops team to manually reconcile balances on every card change — the conservative fixed rate protects Capital One from customers gaming the direction of conversion for value.

sources.label: AwardWallet - Convert Capital One Cash Back to Transferrable Miles
Capital One - What Is a Credit Card Product Change?

records.title: Chase Ultimate Rewards
records.summary: Chase's shared points program that carries a cardmember's balance automatically across Ultimate Rewards-earning cards, while gating redemption value by current card tier.

data.positioning: Chase presents Ultimate Rewards as one shared, flexible points program that stays with the cardmember across their Chase cards, rather than a balance tied to any single card product.

scores.axis: Manual operations involvement in reward continuity during upgrade
scores.rationale: research-source-2026-08-11-chase-points-carry-over-product-change describes the points balance carrying over automatically on product change with no manual transfer step described in issuer or third-party guidance.

records.title: American Express Membership Rewards
records.summary: Amex's rewards currency, kept walled off from its cash-back cards at the product-change level.

data.positioning: Amex frames upgrades and downgrades as moves within the same card 'family,' keeping a cardmember's existing rewards currency and benefits path intact rather than offering a path across cash back and Membership Rewards.

records.title: Citi ThankYou Rewards / AAdvantage cards
records.summary: Citi's two separate reward currencies (ThankYou Points and AAdvantage miles), kept apart at the product-change level per third-party reporting.

data.positioning: Citi treats AAdvantage-branded cards and ThankYou Points-branded cards as two separate reward programs that a cardmember must choose between at application, not a single upgrade ladder a customer can move across.

records.title: Capital One Rewards (cash back & miles)
records.summary: Capital One's self-service, one-directional bridge between its cash-back and miles currencies.

data.positioning: Capital One frames 'Combine Rewards' as something the cardmember initiates themselves to move cash back into miles, rather than a conversion the issuer performs automatically for them.

scores.axis: Manual operations involvement in reward continuity during upgrade
scores.rationale: research-source-2026-08-11-capital-one-one-way-cash-to-miles-conversion describes a self-service, customer-initiated conversion with no manual ops step, but it requires the cardmember to hold both a cash back and a miles card and take explicit action, rather than the balance carrying over automatically by default the way Chase's does — placed one point below Chase's fully-automatic default carryover.

records.title: Strategy recommendation: replace the manual ops transfer with an automated, event-driven transfer service
records.summary: Evaluated three ways to resolve the manual-ops scaling bottleneck (risk-2026-08-11-manual-transfer-does-not-scale) in light of competitor research; recommends building a system-initiated automated transfer service that replaces the manual step while retaining today's per-card balance model, rather than a full unified-ledger redesign or a customer self-service flow.

alternatives_considered.option: Option A — Unify reward points into a single customer-level ledger, decoupled from card product (Chase Ultimate Rewards model). Restructure the balance data model so points belong to the customer, not to any specific card product; an upgrade re-associates which card is linked to the same ledger, so no balance ever moves and there is no transfer step for anyone (ops or automation) to perform.
pros: Fully eliminates the manual transfer step itself (per insight-2026-08-11-manual-ops-transfer) rather than automating around it — follows Chase's fully automatic, no-manual-step model directly (competitor-2026-08-11-chase-ultimate-rewards, research-source-2026-08-11-chase-points-carry-over-product-change).

(strategy-agent's judgment, not evidence) Zero marginal operational cost per upgrade going forward — the strongest possible resolution of risk-2026-08-11-manual-transfer-does-not-scale, since there is no per-upgrade operation left to scale at all.
cons: (strategy-agent's judgment, not evidence) Highest engineering cost of the three options and a one-time, high-risk balance-migration project, since it requires restructuring the existing per-card balance model implied by insight-2026-08-11-manual-ops-transfer.

Redemption-value gating by card tier would need to be rebuilt as a mechanism separate from the balance itself, the way Chase has had to (research-source-2026-08-11-chase-redemption-value-gated-by-tier).
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: (strategy-agent's judgment, not evidence) The scope and cost of a full ledger-model migration is disproportionate to directly resolving risk-2026-08-11-manual-transfer-does-not-scale when Option B resolves the same ops-scaling risk at materially lower engineering cost. Worth revisiting later as a long-term target state — see open_questions.

impact.customer_impact: No friction at all during upgrade — reward balance is simply visible under the new card immediately, matching the seamlessness goal named in assumption-2026-08-11-current-handling-not-seamless. Customers would still see redemption options change based on card tier, per research-source-2026-08-11-chase-redemption-value-gated-by-tier, which would need clear communication to avoid a support spike ((strategy-agent's judgment, not evidence)).
impact.business_impact: (strategy-agent's judgment, not evidence) Removes the ops bottleneck named in risk-2026-08-11-manual-transfer-does-not-scale entirely rather than mitigating it, so ops cost per upgrade drops to zero; carries the largest upfront engineering investment of the three options.
impact.scalability_risk: (strategy-agent's judgment, not evidence) Lowest long-term scalability risk of the three options, because there is no per-upgrade operation of any kind — automated or manual — left to scale; volume growth has zero incremental transfer cost.
impact.long_term_maintainability: (strategy-agent's judgment, not evidence) Removes an entire class of transfer logic and edge cases from the codebase going forward, but the upfront migration of existing per-card balances into a unified ledger is a one-time high-risk data migration project not required by the other two options.

alternatives_considered.option: Option B — Event-driven automated transfer service (system replaces ops, per-card balances retained). Keep today's per-card balance model (per insight-2026-08-11-manual-ops-transfer) but replace the human ops step with an automated service, triggered by the upgrade-completion event, that moves the balance from the old card record to the new one algorithmically.
pros: Directly removes ops from the transfer path named in risk-2026-08-11-manual-transfer-does-not-scale, matching the no-manual-step customer outcome Chase achieves (research-source-2026-08-11-chase-points-carry-over-product-change) without requiring the balance-model migration Option A does.

(strategy-agent's judgment, not evidence) Lower engineering cost and smaller blast radius than Option A, since it automates the existing transfer concept rather than replacing the underlying data model.
cons: (strategy-agent's judgment, not evidence) Retains a per-upgrade transfer operation — now automated rather than manual — as a potential point of failure under concurrency or retries; see the new risk record linked to this decision.
Does not remove the transfer concept from the codebase long-term the way Option A would, so it is a partial rather than complete resolution of the underlying architecture question.

impact.customer_impact: Matches Chase's no-manual-step, no-customer-action outcome (research-source-2026-08-11-chase-points-carry-over-product-change) from the customer's point of view — the balance appears on the new card without the customer taking any action, unlike Capital One's self-service model (research-source-2026-08-11-capital-one-one-way-cash-to-miles-conversion), which requires an explicit customer action.
impact.business_impact: (strategy-agent's judgment, not evidence) Directly removes ops from the critical path named in risk-2026-08-11-manual-transfer-does-not-scale at a lower upfront cost than Option A, since it automates the existing transfer step instead of eliminating the concept of a transfer.
impact.scalability_risk: (strategy-agent's judgment, not evidence) Scales far better than today's manual process, since throughput is no longer bounded by ops headcount (risk-2026-08-11-manual-transfer-does-not-scale), but retains a per-upgrade transfer operation (now automated) as a potential failure point under high volume or concurrency, unlike Option A which removes the operation entirely.
impact.long_term_maintainability: (strategy-agent's judgment, not evidence) Keeps today's per-card balance model, so it's a smaller, more isolated change to maintain than Option A's ledger migration, but the platform will carry transfer/reconciliation logic indefinitely rather than eliminating that class of code.

alternatives_considered.option: Option C — Self-service, customer-initiated transfer step (Capital One 'Combine Rewards' model). Build a customer-facing flow where, at or after upgrade, the customer is prompted to confirm and trigger the points transfer themselves (with a stated fixed rate if crossing reward-currency families), mirroring Capital One's self-service, one-directional conversion.
pros: Lowest engineering cost of the three, closely mirroring Capital One's existing self-service 'Combine Rewards' pattern (competitor-2026-08-11-capital-one-rewards, research-source-2026-08-11-capital-one-one-way-cash-to-miles-conversion) rather than requiring new balance architecture.
Removes ops from the default path named in risk-2026-08-11-manual-transfer-does-not-scale by shifting the action to the customer instead of the system.
cons: (strategy-agent's judgment, not evidence) Adds a manual action for the customer, unlike Chase's fully automatic default (research-source-2026-08-11-chase-points-carry-over-product-change) or Option B above; this runs counter to the seamlessness goal implied by assumption-2026-08-11-current-handling-not-seamless, and risks points sitting un-transferred if customers don't complete the step, echoing how Capital One's conversion only happens when the customer explicitly acts (research-source-2026-08-11-capital-one-one-way-cash-to-miles-conversion).

(strategy-agent's judgment, not evidence) If customers don't complete the self-service step, it risks re-creating an ops escalation path, only partially resolving risk-2026-08-11-manual-transfer-does-not-scale rather than removing it from the default path.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: (strategy-agent's judgment, not evidence) Shifting the transfer action onto the customer runs counter to the seamlessness goal underlying assumption-2026-08-11-current-handling-not-seamless and risks reintroducing an ops escalation path for incomplete transfers, undermining the direct resolution of risk-2026-08-11-manual-transfer-does-not-scale that Option B achieves without that dependency.

impact.customer_impact: (strategy-agent's judgment, not evidence) Adds a manual action for the customer during or after upgrade; runs counter to the seamlessness goal implied by assumption-2026-08-11-current-handling-not-seamless, since the customer must notice and complete a step rather than the balance simply carrying over.
impact.business_impact: (strategy-agent's judgment, not evidence) Removes ops from the default path named in risk-2026-08-11-manual-transfer-does-not-scale at the lowest engineering cost of the three options, but shifts risk from an ops bottleneck to a customer-drop-off/support-ticket risk if customers don't understand or complete the step.
impact.scalability_risk: (strategy-agent's judgment, not evidence) Scales well on the engineering side since it's a self-service flow, but does not fully resolve the underlying scaling risk in risk-2026-08-11-manual-transfer-does-not-scale if a meaningful share of customers abandon or mishandle the self-service step and it lands back with ops as an escalation, unlike Options A and B which remove ops from the default path entirely.
impact.long_term_maintainability: (strategy-agent's judgment, not evidence) Smallest change of the three, but couples the reward-continuity experience to a customer action rather than to a stable backend guarantee, which may need revisiting if adoption/completion rates are poor.

data.recommendation: Option B — build an event-driven, system-initiated automated transfer service that replaces the manual ops step while retaining today's per-card balance data model.
data.rationale: This recommendation directly addresses risk-2026-08-11-manual-transfer-does-not-scale — the manual ops transfer described in insight-2026-08-11-manual-ops-transfer is the named bottleneck, and Option B removes ops from that path entirely by replacing the manual step with an automated, event-driven service, resolving the risk at materially lower engineering cost than Option A's full ledger-model unification while avoiding the customer-completion risk Option C would introduce (see Option C's rejected_because). Removing the manual step, rather than shifting it to the customer, also better serves the seamlessness goal implied by assumption-2026-08-11-current-handling-not-seamless. Unlike Amex and Citi, whose approach to reward continuity (competitor-2026-08-11-american-express-membership-rewards, competitor-2026-08-11-citi-thankyou-rewards) is to restrict which upgrades are even allowed so continuity is trivial by construction, none of the three options considered here restrict upgrade paths: insight-2026-08-11-manual-ops-transfer describes manual transfer as today's universal handling for upgrades generally, not something contingent on crossing a reward-currency boundary, so a restriction-based approach wouldn't by itself resolve risk-2026-08-11-manual-transfer-does-not-scale — it was considered and set aside as a possible fourth option for that reason rather than engineered into any of the three above. This recommendation rests on an unvalidated assumption: that this platform's per-card balance data model (as it exists today per insight-2026-08-11-manual-ops-transfer) can be automated in place without first needing the kind of redesign Option A represents. If that turns out not to be true — e.g., if the current data model doesn't cleanly support an atomic move between card records — Option A may need to be revisited as the real minimum viable path rather than a longer-term one.
open_questions: Does this platform's card upgrades ever cross reward-currency families (e.g., cash-back to points, analogous to what Amex and Citi wall off per competitor-2026-08-11-american-express-membership-rewards and competitor-2026-08-11-citi-thankyou-rewards)? Not established in the store; if yes, Option B's automated service would need a defined conversion rule analogous to Capital One's fixed-rate approach (research-source-2026-08-11-capital-one-one-way-cash-to-miles-conversion) rather than a simple balance move.
Should Option B be treated as a permanent target state, or a stepping stone toward Option A's unified-ledger model longer term? Not decided by this recommendation.

What are this platform's actual per-card balance data model constraints (e.g., can a balance be atomically moved between card records)? This recommendation assumes it can be automated in place; if that assumption is invalidated, Option A becomes the likely fallback.

Is redemption value (e.g., boosted rates, transfer partners) gated by card tier today on this platform the way Chase gates it (research-source-2026-08-11-chase-redemption-value-gated-by-tier), or is redemption value currently uniform across this platform's cards? This affects whether Option B needs equivalent tier-gating logic built alongside the automated transfer.

records.title: Automating the transfer shifts risk from an ops-capacity bottleneck to system-level failure modes
records.summary: Replacing the manual ops transfer with an automated, event-driven service (as recommended in decision-2026-08-11-automated-transfer-service-recommendation) removes the ops-capacity bottleneck described in risk-2026-08-11-manual-transfer-does-not-scale, but introduces a different, currently unaddressed class of risk: retries, idempotency, and partial-transfer states under concurrent or failed upgrade events.
records.details: Surfaced while evaluating automation options for risk-2026-08-11-manual-transfer-does-not-scale: an event-driven automated transfer (Option B in decision-2026-08-11-automated-transfer-service-recommendation) still performs a per-upgrade transfer operation, just without a human in the loop. If the service fails partway through, retries without idempotency protection, or races with a concurrent upgrade/downgrade on the same account, a customer's balance could end up duplicated, lost, or left in an inconsistent state. This is a materially different failure mode than the ops-capacity bottleneck risk-2026-08-11-manual-transfer-does-not-scale describes, and nothing currently in the store addresses it — solution-design should define reconciliation, idempotency, and retry-safety requirements for the automated transfer service before it is built.

records.title: System automatically transfers reward-point balance on upgrade completion
records.summary: When a credit card upgrade completes, the customer's reward-point balance moves from the old card record to the new one automatically, with no manual operations step.

data.statement: The system automatically transfers the full reward-points balance from a customer's prior card record to their new card record when a credit card upgrade completes, without any manual operations action.
acceptance_criteria: When a credit card upgrade completes, the full reward-points balance from the prior card record is present on the new card record with no manual operations action taken.
The customer does not need to take any action beyond completing the upgrade itself for the balance to move.
The sum of the customer's reward points immediately before the transfer equals the sum immediately after — no points are lost or duplicated.
edge_cases: This requirement covers the successful-transfer path only; failure/retry/idempotency behavior is a separate requirement — see requirement-2026-08-11-transfer-idempotency-and-retry-safety.

records.details: decision-2026-08-11-automated-transfer-service-recommendation's own open_questions flags that this recommendation assumes the current per-card balance data model supports moving a balance atomically between card records, and that this is not yet confirmed — if that assumption is invalidated, this requirement (and Option B generally) needs revisiting in favor of Option A's unified-ledger model. Two further open questions from that same decision are deliberately not addressed by this requirement, not silently resolved: whether upgrades ever cross reward-currency families (competitor-2026-08-11-american-express-membership-rewards and competitor-2026-08-11-citi-thankyou-rewards wall this off; this platform's own answer is still unknown), and whether redemption value should be tier-gated the way research-source-2026-08-11-chase-redemption-value-gated-by-tier describes Chase doing it. Both remain open.

records.title: Transfer is triggered only once the new card is fully active
records.summary: The automated transfer is triggered by a single, well-defined event: the new card record reaching active status — not an earlier step like upgrade-requested or approved-but-not-active.

data.statement: The automated transfer service is triggered by exactly one event — the new card record's status becoming "active" — and not by any earlier upgrade-lifecycle event such as upgrade-requested or approved-but-not-yet-active.
acceptance_criteria: No transfer attempt occurs before the new card record's status is "active."
Exactly one triggering event is emitted per upgrade, at the point the new card record becomes active.

records.details: (solution-design's judgment, not evidence) Which exact point in the upgrade lifecycle should trigger the transfer was not specified by decision-2026-08-11-automated-transfer-service-recommendation. Triggering on "active" rather than an earlier event minimizes the chance of transferring points onto a new card record that later fails final provisioning. This is a small implementation choice, not a meaningfully-weighed alternative, so it's resolved here rather than as a new decision record.

records.title: Automated transfer is idempotent and safely retryable
records.summary: The automated transfer service produces exactly one balance transfer per upgrade even if the triggering event is redelivered or a transfer is retried after a partial failure.

data.statement: The automated transfer service is idempotent and safely retryable: if the upgrade-completion event is delivered more than once, or a transfer is retried after a partial failure, the customer's final reward-point balance reflects exactly one transfer — never zero, and never duplicated.
acceptance_criteria: Redelivering the same upgrade-completion event twice results in exactly one balance transfer, not two.
If the transfer service errors or crashes mid-transfer, retrying from the last known state does not double-credit or double-debit either card record.
A transfer that fails partway leaves the system in a state where the inconsistency is detectable, not silent.
edge_cases: risk-2026-08-11-automated-transfer-failure-modes: this requirement exists specifically because that risk identified that replacing manual ops with automation trades an ops-capacity bottleneck for retry/idempotency/partial-transfer risk. This requirement addresses the idempotency and retry-safety part of that risk; it does not cover operational monitoring or alerting for stuck/failed transfers, which remains unaddressed and is a candidate for a future systems-impact assessment, not something resolved here.

records.title: The "new card active" trigger likely isn't a published, redeliverable event yet
records.summary: requirement-2026-08-11-transfer-trigger-event's trigger point and requirement-2026-08-11-transfer-idempotency-and-retry-safety's redelivery handling both presuppose an event that, per the store's own description of today's fully manual process, doesn't appear to exist as a subscribable event yet.

data.impact_description: requirement-2026-08-11-transfer-trigger-event specifies the transfer service is triggered by the new card record's status becoming "active," and requirement-2026-08-11-transfer-idempotency-and-retry-safety's acceptance criteria explicitly require handling the case where "the upgrade-completion event is delivered more than once." Both assume a genuine, subscribable event with at-least-once delivery and redelivery semantics already exists at that point in the upgrade lifecycle. insight-2026-08-11-manual-ops-transfer establishes that today's transfer is a fully manual ops action, with nothing in the store indicating card-status-becoming-active is currently published as an event rather than just a status column update inside the upgrade flow. If it isn't already an emitted event, standing one up — with the delivery and redelivery guarantees requirement-3 depends on — is new event infrastructure the automated transfer service is being built on top of, not something it can simply subscribe to.

records.title: Idempotency and detectability require a persisted per-upgrade transfer record, not just balance columns
records.summary: Satisfying requirement-2026-08-11-transfer-idempotency-and-retry-safety's exactly-once and detectable-not-silent acceptance criteria requires a new, queryable transfer-attempt entity keyed by upgrade — something the current per-card balance model, built for a human-mediated process, has no reason to already have.

data.impact_description: requirement-2026-08-11-transfer-idempotency-and-retry-safety requires that redelivering the same upgrade-completion event twice results in exactly one transfer, and that a partial failure leaves the inconsistency "detectable, not silent." Neither is achievable from the balance columns alone (per requirement-2026-08-11-automated-balance-transfer-on-upgrade) — the service needs a separate, persisted record per upgrade attempt (e.g., keyed by the triggering event or upgrade id) tracking status such as pending/complete/failed, so a redelivered event can be recognized as already-handled and a partial failure has somewhere to be flagged. insight-2026-08-11-manual-ops-transfer describes today's process as a human performing the transfer directly, with no indication such a record already exists — a person doing the move by hand didn't need one.

records.title: "Detectable" inconsistency still needs something actively looking for it
records.summary: requirement-2026-08-11-transfer-idempotency-and-retry-safety only requires a partial-transfer inconsistency to be detectable in principle; its own edge_cases explicitly scope out alerting or monitoring for it, so nothing yet ensures anyone is notified when that state occurs.

data.impact_description: requirement-2026-08-11-transfer-idempotency-and-retry-safety's third acceptance criterion only requires that a partial failure leave the system in a state where the inconsistency is "detectable, not silent" — and its own edge_cases entry explicitly states this requirement "does not cover operational monitoring or alerting for stuck/failed transfers, which remains unaddressed." Detectable in stored state and actually detected are different things: without an alert or scheduled check that surfaces a flagged inconsistency to a person, a customer's transfer can sit in that technically-detectable-but-unobserved state indefinitely, with the wrong balance showing on their new card the whole time.

records.details: This is severe enough that it likely needs a follow-up requirement — e.g. an active alert or reconciliation check on any transfer left in a non-terminal or failed state past an expected window — but writing that requirement is out of scope here.

records.title: Automating the transfer removes ops from the default path but defines no exception handoff
records.summary: Ops previously performed and therefore always knew the state of every transfer; once the automated service handles the default path, no requirement here defines who receives a flagged inconsistency or what they do with it.

data.impact_description: insight-2026-08-11-manual-ops-transfer establishes that operations previously performed every reward-point transfer by hand, which meant they inherently knew the state of every in-flight transfer. requirement-2026-08-11-automated-balance-transfer-on-upgrade and requirement-2026-08-11-transfer-idempotency-and-retry-safety together remove ops from that path under the normal case, and the latter anticipates transfers can still fail partway — but neither requirement, nor anything else in the store, defines who receives a flagged inconsistency once one is detected, or what action they're expected to take. Ops's role changes from "performs every transfer" to "resolves an unspecified subset of exceptions," with no defined handoff or runbook for the first stuck transfer after launch.

records.title: Support loses its informal visibility into transfer status once ops is out of the loop
records.summary: A customer's first sign of a problem is missing points on their new card, and support agents no longer have an ops person to ask what happened, since no requirement here gives them a way to look up an individual transfer's status.

data.impact_description: requirement-2026-08-11-automated-balance-transfer-on-upgrade's acceptance criteria state the customer takes no action beyond the upgrade itself, so a customer's first signal that something went wrong is simply noticing their points are missing after upgrading. insight-2026-08-11-manual-ops-transfer describes today's transfer as a manual ops action, meaning a support agent fielding a "where are my points" question could previously ask the ops person who performed it directly. Once the transfer is automated per this decision, none of the three requirements define a way for a support agent to look up an individual customer's transfer status (pending/complete/failed) — automating the transfer removes that informal visibility path without replacing it with anything support-facing.

records.title: A detectable inconsistency is not the same as a monitored one
records.summary: requirement-2026-08-11-transfer-idempotency-and-retry-safety makes a partial-transfer inconsistency detectable in the system's state, but nothing in the store defines an alert, an owner, or a resolution process for it, so a flagged inconsistency could persist unnoticed and unresolved indefinitely despite technically satisfying that requirement's "detectable, not silent" criterion.
records.details: This is distinct from risk-2026-08-11-automated-transfer-failure-modes, which was about the existence of retry/idempotency/partial-transfer failure modes themselves and is what requirement-2026-08-11-transfer-idempotency-and-retry-safety was written to address. This new risk is one step further downstream: even with that requirement satisfied, satisfying "detectable" only means the information exists somewhere in stored state — it says nothing about whether anyone is watching for it, alerted to it, or has an owner for resolving it once flagged (system-impact-2026-08-11-monitoring-detectable-not-monitored, system-impact-2026-08-11-operations-no-exception-handoff).
